# How is the code laid out?

*You'll need the round's loop (chapter 1), the order book and orders (chapter 2), fill models (chapter 6) and the
portal's figures and penalty (chapter 8).*

## The story

The third rehearsal, the Kestrel Bourse, hid a rule: orders reached the exchange one step after the bot sent them.
Two agent sessions played it, one with the repo before its calibration tools and one after. Both worked out the hidden rules
soon after their first upload. Both lost money anyway: −4,850 and −283 credits on the public sessions, −3,553 and
−489 on the hidden ones, where the exchange's own plain market maker made +325
[(`IDEAS.md`, "The kickoff prompts on a disguised round")]{.src}.

Most of the loss wasn't the strategy. It was the few lines that turn a strategy's wishes into orders. With orders a step late,
an order sent last step is neither in the book yet nor gone; neither session's code counted those orders "on their way".
So each step it saw no order where it wanted one, sent another, ran into the exchange's cap of three working orders,
and, when the late orders all arrived, held more than its limit and paid the penalty. Counting the orders on their way,
and changing nothing else, took the public score from −283 to +142, the hidden one from −489 to −389, and the hidden
days' penalty from 25 to 0. What was left was a choice of settings: one product was quoted at all, under a matching
rule that made quoting it lose [(`IDEAS.md`, "The kickoff prompts on a disguised round")]{.src}. The sessions' bots
lacked the counting in the code between the strategy and the exchange; the template now does it in EXECUTION
(`on_the_way` and `went`), switched on by the ADAPTER's `DELAY`.

That is why the bot is split the way it is.

## The idea

### The engine knows no format

@fig-architecture is the repo on one page.

![The repo's architecture. A format plug-in turns any exchange's data into Days of Ticks, and wraps the bot's call;
the engine and every tool work only on those. Drawn from `docs/guidebook/research/repo_map.md`, A.](../figures/f13_architecture.png){#fig-architecture
fig-alt="Boxes and arrows: the day's data goes through a format plug-in into Days of Ticks, which feed the engine; the bot file, wrapped by the plug-in, also feeds the engine; the engine feeds backtest, grid, stress, validate and calibrate; diagnose reads the Days directly; a Rust twin of the engine sits beside it."}

- **The engine** (`python/arena/engine.py`) replays a `Day` against a bot and returns fills and PnL. It knows nothing
  about any exchange: no file layout, no bot interface, no units.
- **A format plug-in** (`python/arena/formats/<name>.py`) knows one exchange. It reads that exchange's files into Days,
  wraps the exchange's bot interface so the engine can call it, and states the engine settings the exchange's rules
  fix (resting orders, the mark, delay, fees). On the day the Arena gets its own plug-in, `qminers.py`, already
  sketched with `TODO(day)` markers.
- **The tools** (`arena.backtest`, `arena.grid`, `arena.stress`, `arena.validate`, `arena.diagnose`,
  `experiments.day.calibrate` and the day's experiments) all take `--format` and `--data`, and work on any exchange
  that has a plug-in.

So a new exchange costs a plug-in and an adapter, not a new set of tools. Chapter 1's rehearsal wrote both in about five
minutes.

### The bot in three parts

The template, `python/bots/template.py`, is one self-contained file, as the competitions require, in three sections:

- **STRATEGY** decides what the bot *wants*: for each product, a fair value (chapter 3), then *take* (cross the book
  where it is mispriced against the fair), *clear* (trade back towards zero at the fair when the position is large),
  and *make* (quote either side of the fair). Other modes trade towards a target instead: a level the price returns
  to, a basket's spread, an option's model price, a trader worth following. Every choice is a parameter in `PARAMS`,
  one entry per product, over shared `DEFAULTS`.
- **EXECUTION** turns what the strategy wants into orders and cancels, given what already rests, what is on its way,
  and the limits. This is the part the Kestrel story was about. It is generic, the same on every exchange.
- **ADAPTER** is the only code that knows the exchange: it reads the exchange's state into the template's own form,
  and writes its orders back in the exchange's format. On the day it is the part that changes.

Keeping the three apart is what lets one strategy run on every exchange we have rehearsed, and what keeps an execution bug from hiding
inside strategy code, where the Kestrel sessions looked for it first.

### The rest of the repo

- **The Rust twins** (`rust/`): the engine, the simulator, the statistics and the bots ported to Rust, giving the same
  results to the bit, about 130 times faster per backtest and 40 to 80 times for a whole grid
  [(`rust/README.md`)]{.src}. `--engine rust` uses them; a twin whose Python changed since it was
  checked is refused.
- **`IDEAS.md`**: every idea tested on Prosperity data, with the command and the numbers, kept even when it failed
  ("dropped here"): priors to re-test on the Arena's data, not verdicts.
- **The wiki** (`references/wiki/`): concept pages that join the literature, the other teams' write-ups and our
  measurements, each line cited.
- **The day's documents**: `RUNBOOK.md` (one page), `ON_THE_DAY.md` (every open question, with what to assume and
  what changes if it's different) and `KICKOFF_PROMPT.md` (what starts an agent session).

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
The split is the one between a model, its inference wrapper and a data loader. The engine is the evaluation harness,
plug-ins are dataset loaders behind one interface, STRATEGY is the model, EXECUTION is the serving logic, and ADAPTER is
the input and output layer for one deployment target. As with serving code, the last two are the hardest to test
offline: a replay with no delay can't show an order-counting bug that only a delay exposes. Where the analogy breaks:
a model's serving layer rarely changes the model's results, while here EXECUTION decides which orders exist at all,
so it is part of the strategy's measured performance.
:::

- The template's sections: search `template.py` for `STRATEGY`, `EXECUTION` and `ADAPTER`; `on_the_way` and `went`
  count orders on their way.
- `arena.validate` replays the bot one step late by default (`--late STEPS` changes it), to catch the Kestrel bug
  before an upload.
